newsitem.title: USA: UK budget shows rate hikes coming -U.S. analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK budget shows rate hikes coming -U.S. analysts.

text.p: Modest fiscal tightening and robust economic forecasts in the first UK budget outline from the new Labour party government foretell higher interest rates and a stronger British pound, U.S. analysts said.
The Bank of England's new monetary policy council could raise official rates as soon as next week during its scheduled meeting, analysts said.

"This is a fairly tight budget, but it doesn't do enough in the near term to slow the economy down. The Bank of England could certainly go next week," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities.

Finance Minister Gordon Brown outlined tax increases of $9.1 billion (5.5 billion pounds) this year and $7.9 billion (4.75 billion pounds) next year, but analysts said that will hardly curb the British consumer feast.
"Clearly, there wasn't a lot here aimed at slowing down the pace of consumer spending, which is one of the BoE's biggest concerns," said Sandy Batten, international economist at Citibank.
Brown forecast British gross domestic product growth of 3.25 percent this year and 2.5 percent in 1998, but with consumption growing by at least four percent a year.

Analysts argued that Labour leaders opted for the easy way out, choosing to let the Bank of England take the heat rather than waffle on their election promises not to raise income tax rates or take other steps to meaningfully slow the economy.
"The market may have expected them to be a little gutsier than they were, but they proved not to be so brave," Batten said.
As a result, the pound could continue to surge toward three marks and $1.72 in coming sessions, analysts said.
By late U.S. afternoon, sterling/mark had risen over five pfennigs on the day to as high as 2.9385. Cable was also up two cents to $1.6770.
Yet barring any fresh surprises in the interim, sterling may camp near current levels until next week, analysts said.

"The $64,000 question is how much more do they have to raise rates to calm their inflation concerns, because the market has already built in a high degree of probability they'll go next week," said Batten.
Brown paid lip service to industrial Britain's concerns that the vigorous pound is hampering exports, saying he would address that problem.
But analysts scoffed at this assertion.
"I'm not quite sure what he can do about it. He's already played his cards on the budget and he doesn't have control over monetary policy anymore," Batten said.
In fact, sterling is unlikely to reverse course until the economy shows enough weakness to warrant lower interest rates, analysts said.
"They need to slow the economy down as quickly as possible and then get interest rates down. There's nothing else Brown can do, and I was surprised to see that comment," said Iggo.
